summary: RPL uses Objective Functions to decide how nodes select and optimize routes. This RFC specifies Objective Function Zero, a basic one that works with the default RPL framework and does not need particular metrics.

plainLanguage.summary: RPL is the routing protocol used in low-power mesh networks. It needs a rule for deciding which neighbour to send traffic through on the way to the root, and this RFC defines the simplest workable rule, one that any two implementations can agree on without extra measurements.

questions: how does rpl choose a parent
what is rpl objective function zero
subtitle: The default rule a low-power mesh network uses to pick a path towards its root.

tldr.problem: RPL leaves the choice of route to an Objective Function, and the main specification defines none. Two implementations that pick different objectives cannot form a shared topology.
tldr.mechanism: OF0 is a default objective function. It turns each link into a step of rank, lets the implementation scale and weight that step, and compares candidate parents by an ordered list of criteria ending with the one that produces the smallest Rank.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from March 2012 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It is registered as Objective Code Point 0 and deliberately ignores metric containers, so it needs no extra information from the network.

facts.label: Step of rank
facts.value: A default of 3, with a permitted range from 1 to 9

facts.label: Rank stretch
facts.value: A maximum of 5, with a default of 0

facts.label: Rank factor
facts.value: From 1 to 4, with a default of 1

facts.label: Hop range in the default settings
facts.value: A minimum of 28 hops and a maximum of 255 hops

today: RFC 6552 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2012, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. OF0 is registered as Objective Code Point 0 in the registry RFC 6550 describes, and it deliberately ignores metric containers, so it needs no information beyond what the main RPL specification already exchanges.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks specification, RFC 6550, defines a generic Distance Vector protocol that is adapted to a variety of Low-Power and Lossy Network types by the application of specific Objective Functions.

A RPL Objective Function states the outcome of the process used by a RPL node to select and optimize routes within a RPL Instance based on the Information Objects available. As a general concept, an objective function is not an algorithm. Outside RPL, shortest path first is an objective function where the least cost path between two points is derived as an outcome, and there are a number of algorithms that can be used to satisfy it, of which the well-known Dijkstra algorithm is an example.

The separation of objective functions from the core protocol specification allows RPL to be adapted to meet the different optimization criteria required by the wide range of deployments, applications and network designs.

RPL forms Directed Acyclic Graphs as collections of Destination-Oriented DAGs within instances of the protocol. Each instance is associated with a specialized objective function. A DODAG is periodically reconstructed as a new DODAG Version to enable a global reoptimization of the graph. An instance of RPL running on a device uses the objective function to help it determine which DODAG and which version of that DODAG it should join, and to select a number of routers to serve as parents or as feasible successors.

The RPL Instance uses the objective function to compute a Rank for the device, an abstract distance to the root of the DODAG within the DODAG Version. The Rank is exchanged between nodes and allows other RPL nodes to avoid loops and verify forward progression toward the destination. Regardless of the objective function used, Rank always increases, so after convergence loop-free paths are always formed.

OF0 operates on parameters obtained from provisioning, the RPL DODAG Configuration option and the RPL DODAG Information Object base container. The RPL specification requires the use of a common objective function by all nodes in a network, and it includes no objective function definitions of its own. Because there is no default objective function or metric container in the main specification, two implementations that do not follow the same guidance will not support a common objective function with which they could interoperate.

OF0 is designed as a default objective function that allows interoperation between implementations across a wide spectrum of use cases. This is why it does not specify how link properties are transformed into a rank increase and leaves that to the implementation. Instead it enforces the values for the rank increase by normalizing the step of rank for a normal link and its acceptable range, rather than formulating the details of the computation. This is also why OF0 ignores metric containers.
sections.plainLanguage: An objective function says what a good route looks like, and the protocol figures out how to find one. OF0 is the simplest such rule: it only counts steps, so two devices that both implement it will agree on the shape of the network without exchanging any extra measurements.

sections.title: Objective Function Zero Overview
sections.content:
The RPL specification describes constraints on how nodes select potential parents, a parent set, from their neighbours. All parents are feasible successors for upward traffic towards the root. RPL also allows the use of parents in a subsequent version of the same DODAG as feasible successors, in which case the node acts as a leaf in that subsequent version.

The goal of OF0 is for a node to join a DODAG Version that offers good enough connectivity to a specific set of nodes or to a larger routing infrastructure, though there is no guarantee that the path will be optimized according to a specific metric. The validation of that connectivity is implementation and link type dependent and is out of scope. For the purpose of OF0, the term Grounded means that the DODAG root provides such connectivity; how that connectivity is asserted and maintained is out of scope.

Objective Function Zero is designed to find the nearest Grounded root. This can be achieved if the Rank of a node is very close to an abstract function of its distance to the root. That need is balanced against the other need of maintaining some path diversity, which may be achieved by increasing the Rank. In the absence of a Grounded root, inner connectivity within the network is still desirable, and floating DAGs will form, rooted at the nodes with the highest administrative preference.

OF0 selects a preferred parent and a backup feasible successor if one is available. All the upward traffic is normally routed via the preferred parent, with no attempt at load balancing. When the link conditions do not let an upward packet through the preferred parent, the packet is passed to the backup feasible successor.

A RPL node monitors links to a number of neighbour nodes and can use OF0 to assign a rank increase to each link. The exact method for computing the rank increase is implementation dependent, but the computation must follow the rules in Section 4.1.
sections.plainLanguage: The objective is to reach a root that has a way out to the rest of the network, and to reach the closest such root. A second path is kept as a spare. If there is no root with a way out at all, the network still forms a shape of its own around whichever node is configured to be preferred.

sections.title: Computing Rank
sections.content:
An OF0 implementation first computes a variable step_of_rank associated with a given parent, from relevant link properties and metrics. The step of rank is used to compute the amount by which to increase the Rank along a particular link.

Computing a step of rank based on a static metric such as an administrative cost implies that the implementation only considers parents with good enough connectivity, and produces a Rank analogous to a hop count. In most low-power networks this favours paths with fewer but longer hops of poorer connectivity, so it is recommended to base the computation on dynamic link properties such as the expected transmission count metric discussed in RFC 6551. The document on the Minimum Rank Objective Function with Hysteresis gives further guidance on how link cost can be computed and how hysteresis can improve Rank stability.

OF0 allows an implementation to stretch the step of rank in order to enable the selection of at least one feasible successor and thus maintain path diversity. Stretching is not recommended, because it augments the apparent distance from the node to the root, distorts the DODAG from its optimal shape, and may cause instabilities through greedy behaviour in which depending nodes augment their Ranks to use each other as parents in a loop. An implementation may stretch the step of rank by at most a configurable stretch_of_rank of any value between 0, meaning no stretch, and the fixed constant MAXIMUM_RANK_STRETCH. The stretched step of rank must be kept between the fixed constants MINIMUM_STEP_OF_RANK and MAXIMUM_STEP_OF_RANK, a range that allows the reflection of a large variation of link quality.

The gap between MINIMUM_STEP_OF_RANK and MAXIMUM_RANK_STRETCH may not be enough to strongly distinguish links of different types, for example to favour powered over battery-operated links, or high-speed wired over lower-speed wireless links, within the same DAG. An implementation should allow the operator to configure a factor called rank_factor and apply it to all links and peers, to multiply the effect of the stretched step of rank in the rank increase computation. An implementation may recognise categories of peers and links and configure a more specific rank_factor for those categories, and the rank_factor must be set between MINIMUM_RANK_FACTOR and MAXIMUM_RANK_FACTOR.

The rank increase is represented in units expressed by the variable MinHopRankIncrease, which defaults to the fixed constant DEFAULT_MIN_HOP_RANK_INCREASE of RFC 6550. With that setting, the least significant octet in the RPL Rank field in the DIO Base Object is not used. The step of rank Sp computed for a link is multiplied by the rank factor Rf and then possibly stretched by a term Sr that is less than or equal to the configured stretch_of_rank. The resulting rank increase is added to the Rank of the preferred parent R(P) to obtain that of this node R(N).

By default OF0 encodes the 2-octet Rank in units of 256, and the default settings allow for a minimum of 28, worst acceptable, hops and a maximum of 255, excellent, hops.

Optionally, the administrative preference of a root may be configured to supersede the goal of joining a Grounded DODAG. In that case nodes associate with the root with the highest preference available, regardless of whether that root is Grounded. Compared with a deployment with a multitude of Grounded roots, which would result in the same multitude of DODAGs, such a configuration may result in fewer but larger DODAGs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each link gets a number describing how much it costs to step along it. The number can be scaled up by a factor the operator sets, and can be stretched a little to open up a second path. A node's Rank is its parent's Rank plus that scaled number, so Ranks grow as you move away from the root and no two nodes can claim to be each other's parent.

sections.title: Parent and Backup Selection
sections.content:
Preferred parent. As OF0 scans all the candidate neighbours it keeps the parent that is best according to the following criteria, in order. First, a candidate that would not satisfy the generic re-parenting rules of Section 8 of RFC 6550, including the boundaries for augmenting its Rank within a DODAG Version, must not be considered. Second, before selecting a router as the preferred parent, an implementation should validate the connectivity and suitability of the router, which involves checking the Layer 2 connectivity to the router, the Layer 3 connectivity it offers, and may involve other factors such as locally or globally configured policies. In most cases a router that does not pass validation cannot be considered further, and a router that did pass should be preferred over one that did not. Third, when multiple interfaces are available, a locally configured policy might order them, and that policy applies first. Fourth, if the administrative preference of the root is configured to supersede the goal of joining a Grounded DODAG, a router that offers connectivity to a more preferable root should be preferred. Fifth, a router that offers connectivity to a grounded DODAG Version should be preferred over one that does not. Sixth, a router that offers connectivity to a more preferable root should be preferred. Seventh, when comparing two parents that belong to the same DODAG, a router that offers connectivity to the most recent DODAG Version should be preferred. Eighth, the parent that causes the lesser resulting Rank for this node should be preferred. Ninth, a DODAG Version for which there is an alternate parent should be preferred; this check is optional and is performed by computing the backup feasible successor while assuming that the router currently being examined is finally selected as preferred parent. Tenth, the preferred parent that was in use already should be preferred. Eleventh, a router that has announced a DIO message more recently should be preferred.

These rules and their order may be varied by an implementation according to configured policy.

Backup feasible successor. The OF performs these checks in order. The backup feasible successor must not be the preferred parent. It must be either in the same DODAG Version as this node or in a subsequent DODAG Version. Along with the RPL rules, a router in the same DODAG Version as this node with a Rank higher than the Rank computed for this node must not be selected. A router with a lesser Rank should be preferred. A router that has been validated as usable by the implementation should be preferred. When multiple interfaces are available, a router on a higher order interface is preferable. The backup feasible successor that was in use already should be preferred. These rules and their order may also be varied by an implementation according to configured policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Choosing a parent is a fixed checklist: the candidate has to be legal for RPL, it has to actually work, the interface it is on may have a local preference, and only then are the root, the graph version and the resulting Rank compared. The spare parent follows a shorter list, with the same Rank and validation checks.

sections.title: The Abstract Interface to OF0
sections.content:
Objective Function Zero interacts with the RPL core for its management and operations in four ways.

When a new DIO is received, the objective function that corresponds to the Objective Code Point in the DIO is triggered with the content of the DIO. OF0 is identified by OCP 0. The OF0 support provides an interface that returns information about a given instance, including material from the DIO base header, the role, whether router or leaf, and the Rank of this node. It provides an interface that returns the ordered list of parents and feasible successors for a given instance to the RPL core, including the material contained in the transit option for each entry. And it provides events to inform it that a change in DAG information or in the parent list has occurred, which can be caused by an interaction with another system component such as configuration, timers or device drivers, and which may cause the RPL core to fire a new DIO or reset Trickle timers.
sections.plainLanguage: OF0 plugs into RPL through four hooks: it is told when a new graph description arrives, it reports the graph details, it reports the ordered list of parents, and it is told when something else in the device changed the graph.

sections.title: OF0 Operands
sections.content:
On top of the variables and constants defined in RFC 6550, OF0 introduces the following.

The variables are step_of_rank, a strictly positive integer that is an intermediate computation based on the link properties with a certain neighbour, and rank_increase, a strictly positive integer that is the delta between the Rank of the preferred parent and self.

The configurable parameters are stretch_of_rank, an unsigned integer giving the maximum augmentation to the step of rank of a preferred parent to allow the selection of an additional feasible successor, where a value of zero means the step of rank is not stretched; and rank_factor, a strictly positive integer used to multiply the effect of the link properties in the rank increase computation, where a value of 1 is used if none is configured.

The constants are fixed by this specification and are listed in the table below.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things can be tuned: how much a step costs, how much the whole step is multiplied by, and how far it may be stretched. The table gives the limits each one has to stay inside.

sections.title: Manageability Considerations
sections.content:
Section 18 of RFC 6550 depicts the management of the protocol. This specification inherits that section and its subsections, with the exception that the metrics specified in RFC 6551 are not used and do not require management.

Device configuration. An implementation should allow the configuration of at least a global rank_factor that applies to all links, and may allow the grouping of interfaces, links or neighbours with a more specific rank_factor for such groups. It may allow the configuration of a maximum stretch_of_rank that must be less than or equal to MAXIMUM_RANK_STRETCH; if none is configured a value of 0 is assumed and the step of rank is not stretched.

An OF0 implementation should support the DODAG Configuration option of Section 6.7.6 of RFC 6550 and apply the parameters it contains. The parameters are configured to the nodes that may become DODAG roots, and the nodes redistribute the information using that option. In particular, the value of MinHopRankIncrease can be distributed with the option and overrides the fixed constant DEFAULT_MIN_HOP_RANK_INCREASE of Section 17 of RFC 6550, which has a fixed value of 256.

Out of the box, at initial factory time, the default constant values should be used: the rank_factor is set to DEFAULT_RANK_FACTOR, the maximum stretch_of_rank is set to DEFAULT_RANK_STRETCH, and the MinHopRankIncrease is set to DEFAULT_MIN_HOP_RANK_INCREASE. The values can be overridden at any time and apply at the next version of the DODAG.

Device monitoring. The OF support must be able to provide information about its operations and trigger events when that information changes. At a minimum the information should include the DAG information of Section 6.3.1 of RFC 6550, covering the DODAGID, the RPLInstanceID, the Mode of Operation, the Rank of this node, the current Version Number and the value of the Grounded flag; and a list of neighbours indicating the preferred parent and an alternate feasible successor if available, with the Rank, the current Version Number and the value of the Grounded flag for each neighbour.
sections.plainLanguage: An operator can set the scaling and stretching values on the device, and the root can push them out to the whole network with the standard configuration option. The device should also be able to report the current graph, its Rank and its parent list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This specification makes simple extensions to RPL, so it is vulnerable to and benefits from the security issues and mechanisms described in RFC 6550 and in the security framework for routing over low-power and lossy networks. The document introduces no new flows and no new messages, so it requires no specific mitigation for new threats.

OF0 depends on information exchanged in the Rank and Objective Code Point protocol elements. If those elements were compromised, an implementation of OF0 might generate the wrong path for a packet, resulting in it being misrouted. Deployments are therefore recommended to use the RPL security mechanisms if there is a risk that routing information might be modified or spoofed.
sections.plainLanguage: OF0 adds no messages of its own, so it inherits whatever protection RPL has. The one thing to watch is that a spoofed Rank could send packets down the wrong path.

viz.caption: The terms OF0 uses for the shape of the network

items.title: DODAG
items.text: A directed acyclic graph of nodes with a single root, rebuilt periodically as a new version so the whole shape can be improved.

items.title: Rank
items.text: An abstract distance to the root, exchanged between nodes so they can avoid loops and check forward progress.

items.title: Grounded
items.text: The root provides connectivity to the wider network. How it does so is out of scope.

items.title: Preferred parent
items.text: The neighbour that all upward traffic normally goes through.

items.title: Backup feasible successor
items.text: The second choice, used when the preferred parent's link will not carry the packet.

viz.caption: The rank increase computation, as given in the RFC

data.title: Computing the Rank of a node
data.code:
R(N) = R(P) + rank_increase

rank_increase = (Rf*Sp + Sr) * MinHopRankIncrease

viz.caption: The preferred parent criteria, in the order the RFC gives them

items.label: Legal for RPL
items.desc: A candidate that breaks the generic re-parenting rules of RFC 6550 must not be considered.

items.label: Connectivity validated
items.desc: The router's Layer 2 and Layer 3 connectivity is checked, along with any local or global policy.

items.label: Interface order
items.desc: A locally configured policy may order the interfaces, and it applies first.

items.label: Administrative preference
items.desc: If the root preference is configured to override the Grounded goal, a more preferable root wins.

items.label: Grounded DODAG
items.desc: A router offering connectivity to a grounded DODAG Version is preferred.

items.label: More preferable root
items.desc: A router offering connectivity to a more preferable root is preferred.

items.label: Most recent version
items.desc: Between two parents in the same DODAG, the one in the most recent DODAG Version is preferred.

items.label: Lesser resulting Rank
items.desc: The parent that produces the smaller Rank for this node is preferred.

items.label: Alternate parent available
items.desc: An optional check, performed by computing the backup feasible successor.

items.label: Keep the current parent
items.desc: The preferred parent already in use is preferred.

items.label: More recent DIO
items.desc: A router that announced a DIO message more recently is preferred.
